title: Ankara Unveils $5.2B Manufacturing Financing Package as July Trade Data Show Widening Deficit; Somalia Drilling Ahead of Schedule
subhead: Turkey's industrial policy shifts into high gear with a 250 billion lira employment-linked loan package, while official data show exports rising slower than imports and a 13% jump in the energy import bill. The Kurdish peace process board set its roadmap and Turkish deep-sea drilling off Somalia is running a month ahead of plan.

sections.heading: Economy: Ankara unveils $5.2B manufacturing financing package
sections.body: Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır announced a 250 billion lira ($5.18 billion) employment-linked financing package for manufacturers on Aug. 28, with applications opening Sept. 1, per Hürriyet Daily News. Loans carry maturities of up to 36 months; fixed-rate loans start at an annual cost of 37 percent, but the ministry covers 12 percentage points for firms that hold their January-June employment levels through the second half of 2026, bringing the effective rate down to as low as 25 percent. The credit ceiling for large companies rises from 50 million to 150 million liras, with SMEs getting credit-guarantee support.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a targeted state intervention to shield industrial employment as domestic demand cools — an explicit bet that credit can be steered toward production without reigniting inflation, and a signal of Ankara's political priority on manufacturing jobs ahead of the Medium-Term Program due Sept. 7.

sections.heading: Economy: Exports rise but deficit widens as energy bill jumps 13%
sections.body: Official data released Aug. 28 showed exports up 2.9 percent year-on-year to $25.62 billion in July while imports rose faster, 5.1 percent to $32.97 billion, widening the trade deficit 13.6 percent to $7.34 billion, according to TÜİK and the Trade Ministry figures reported by Hürriyet Daily News. The energy import bill climbed 13.1 percent to $5.83 billion for the month, underlining the pressure from the Iran-war supply shock. Germany remained the top export market ($2.04B), followed by the U.S. ($1.68B), while China ($5.04B) and Russia ($3.23B) led imports. High-tech goods reached 4.4 percent of manufacturing exports, up from 4.2 percent.
sections.whyItMatters: The deficit widening and surge in energy costs are the clearest data readout yet of how the regional war and supply diversification are squeezing Turkey's external balance — and they frame the CBRT's cautious easing path and the new state financing push.

sections.heading: Kurdish peace process: monitoring board sets its roadmap
sections.body: Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said the new Monitoring and Evaluation Board under the 'terror-free Türkiye' initiative established a roadmap at its inaugural meeting, chaired by Yılmaz on Aug. 24 and reported Aug. 27. 'Our security councils and relevant institutions will make very clear assessments regarding concrete developments on the ground,' Yılmaz said in Ağrı. The board was created under the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration, passed Aug. 10 with 467 votes in favour. Yılmaz also welcomed the SDF's dissolution in Syria, stressing Ankara's interest in 'a stable Syria' with territorial integrity, per Hürriyet Daily News.
sections.whyItMatters: The roadmap formalizes high-level state coordination for implementation of the PKK disarmament process — the phase after the June 2025 disbanding pledge — and pairs it with explicit Turkish endorsement of the parallel Syrian Kurdish integration, linking the two tracks.

sections.heading: Energy: Somalia deep-sea drilling running a month ahead of schedule
sections.body: Somali Petroleum Authority Director General Abdulkadir Adan told state news agency SONNA that Turkey's deep-sea drilling off Somalia is ahead of schedule and could finish by end of September rather than October, having reached a depth of about 3,000 meters with no technical setbacks. Turkey's ultra-deepwater drillship Çağrı Bey is working the Curad-1 well, ~370 km offshore Mogadishu, aiming for 7,500 meters total depth, supported by Altan, Korkut and Sancar vessels and Turkish naval assets. About 470–480 personnel are aboard, roughly 20 percent Turkish. This is Turkey's first deep-sea exploration outside its own waters.
sections.whyItMatters: A successful Curad-1 well would be Turkey's flagship entry into overseas upstream energy — a way to hedge against the Hormuz/supply shock and deepen the Ankara-Mogadishu defense-energy partnership in the Horn of Africa.

sections.heading: Energy: Record month for domestic and solar generation
sections.body: Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said July set all-time monthly highs for electricity from domestic sources and solar. Domestic generation hit 24.75 billion kWh, 71.5 percent of total output, while solar rose to 5.37 billion kWh (15.5 percent of supply), beating June's record, and renewables overall supplied 58.2 percent, per ministry data cited by Hürriyet Daily News. Bayraktar framed the momentum as progress 'toward full energy independence.'
sections.whyItMatters: The renewable build-out is the demand-side complement to Turkey's supply-diversification strategy — a structural buffer against volatile fossil-fuel import prices at a time the energy bill is climbing sharply.

sections.heading: Foreign relations: Visa waivers for Syrian diplomats; Erdogan calls African leaders
sections.body: Turkey waived visas for Syrians holding diplomatic passports, including transit and 90-day tourist stays, via a presidential decision signed Aug. 27 by Erdogan and published Aug. 28 in the Official Gazette, per Hürriyet Daily News. Separately, President Erdogan held phone calls on Aug. 27 with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and DRC President Felix Tshisekedi on regional issues. Turkey continues to host about 2.2 million Syrians under temporary protection, though returns have increased since Assad's fall.
sections.whyItMatters: The diplomatic visa waiver consolidates Ankara's role as the new Damascus authorities' strongest external backer — a concrete reciprocity gesture as the Kurdish integration deal and Syria's re-sovereigntization move forward — while the Africa calls extend Turkey's engagement on the continent.

sections.heading: Economy outlook: BofA sees single CBRT rate cut in October
sections.body: Bank of America expects Turkey's central bank to deliver its first and only policy-rate cut of 2026 in October, a 100-basis-point move to 36 percent after September inflation falls to roughly 30–30.5 percent on favorable base effects, per a research note reported by Hürriyet Daily News. BofA sees year-end inflation at 29.5 percent, GDP growth of 2.8 percent this year, and flags that the Sept. 7 Medium-Term Program will shape the 2027 outlook. It noted the CBRT's resumption of one-week repo auctions has already lowered funding costs by 300 bps to 37 percent, while macroprudential rules should keep lending tight.
sections.whyItMatters: The call underscores the CBRT's cautious normalization path — one modest cut this year as it balances declining inflation against geopolitical and energy-price risks, with policy constrained more by expectations than by headline data.

bottomLine: Saturday's brief is economy-led: Ankara answered cooling demand and a widening trade deficit with a 250 billion lira, employment-linked credit package for manufacturers — state-directed lending aimed at protecting industrial jobs without abandoning the anti-inflation line. The July trade data sharpened the picture, with exports up 2.9% but a 13% jump in the energy import bill dragging the deficit 13.6% wider. In parallel, the Kurdish peace process board formalized its implementation roadmap, Turkey's Somalia drilling moved a month ahead of schedule, and Ankara extended new courtesies to Damascus with a diplomatic visa waiver. The common thread is resilience management: cushioning the domestic economy, locking in energy diversification, and cementing regional ties as the Iran-war shock keeps pushing up Turkey's import costs.
sources: Hürriyet Daily News (Kacır financing package; exports/trade data; Yılmaz peace board; Somalia drilling; solar records; BofA rate cut; Syria visa waiver; Syria SDF adviser), SONNA via Hürriyet Daily News
